episodes.subject: Four killed in Zaporizhzhia, a hurricane in Florida, the Arab world's first solo space probe, and what chatbots do to research papers
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-five hundred hours UTC on the tenth of October. Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in Florida, the BBC reports, and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana. In India, thousands of security personnel are deployed as Delhi braces for a so-called cockroach protest, with trains cancelled and dozens of metro stations shut. Nature reports that the United Arab Emirates has completed the Arab world's first solo space probe and set course for an asteroid. And Nature argues that women are talking about menopause, and health systems must listen.

Ukraine and Russia. Russian guided bombs have hit an apartment building in Zaporizhzhia, killing four people and injuring four, the Kyiv Independent reports. The attack came a day after Russian guided aerial bombs struck residential areas of the city on the ninth of October, killing at least one person and injuring seven, including a child, according to regional officials. In Russia, a major fire has been reported at an oil terminal linked to the Novoshakhtinsk refinery after a suspected drone strike, and the outlet ASTRA reported damage to a residential building in Rostov-on-Don.

Frontier compute. Researchers increasingly use ChatGPT to revise their papers, and a new arXiv study finds that recent GPT versions often narrow or even retract the authors' claims. The authors call this defensive writing when the material does not support the change, and test whether the model is correcting overclaiming or writing for an anticipated reviewer. Another benchmark, OpenProblemBench, sets AI eighty-two unresolved problems from mathematics and theoretical physics, each with its research context, assumptions and prior progress, chosen so proposed solutions can be checked fairly clearly.

Quantum desk. The quantum arXiv feed returned no papers this hour, so Nature carries the physics. It reports that semiconductors have been pushed into insulator territory, and it reports the experimental observation of critical topology. Nature also explains how to control where semiconductor crystals start growing. And in chemistry, it reports that RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles.

Consciousness desk. A bioRxiv preprint develops a theory of multi-tasking in the brain: activity during a single task is often described as lying on a low-dimensional manifold, and when a region handles several tasks it may generate several such manifolds. The theory organises competing models and experiments, distinguishing tasks done in sequence from tasks done at the same time. And Nature reports that an early predecessor to mammals could swim, suckle and swallow.

So, this hour's receipts. A hurricane in Florida, a capital braced for protest, an Arab probe bound for an asteroid, and a call to take menopause seriously. Deaths in Zaporizhzhia and fire at a Russian oil terminal. Chatbots that soften scientific claims, open problems as an AI exam, and the brain's way of juggling tasks. episodes.subject: A life-threatening hurricane, a missile-defence deal, peace talks in Miami, and AI that infers how cells change from a single snapshot
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-three hundred hours UTC on the tenth of October. Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in Florida, the BBC reports; the storm took direct aim at the state and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana. The US Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon, an RTX business, a multiyear contract worth up to six point three billion dollars to produce Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors. And Nature reports that NASA has released a trove of Moon data from the historic Artemis II flight, and that woody blankets are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions.

Ukraine and Russia. US, Ukrainian and European officials have discussed ending Russia's war at a meeting in Miami, the Kyiv Independent reports; it coincided with President Trump's announcement that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States and global markets after a call with Vladimir Putin. President Zelensky has sharply criticised that deal, calling it an investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged, the BBC reports.

Frontier compute. Single-cell snapshots can capture a continuum of cell states, but not the dynamics that move cells between them. A new arXiv paper introduces Finsler flow matching, which uses the directional information in a cell-to-cell transition kernel to infer those trajectories, rather than assuming a symmetric geometry. Another paper presents an explainable framework that reads only the column headers of large tables, mapping them to thirty-nine interpretable types, to annotate data and assess its quality before it enters a knowledge graph, when cell values are missing, noisy or unsuitable.

Quantum desk. Nature explains how to control where semiconductor crystals start growing. And on arXiv, a team working toward distributed quantum computing has entangled a trapped barium ion with a silicon-vacancy centre in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. A photon from the ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the diamond cavity and detected, so a single detected photon heralds the entanglement, aiming at kilohertz rates between separate processor modules.

Consciousness desk. How does the visual cortex refine what it sees over time? A bioRxiv team trained recurrent networks on face and object recognition, varying category, identity and pose, and reports that lateral recurrence dynamically refines visual representations for the task at hand. And in head-fixed mice shown nothing but a simple moving bar of light, with no task or reward, a majority of a class of medial entorhinal neurons responded topographically.

So, this hour's receipts. A hurricane ashore in Florida, interceptors for missile defence, Moon data from Artemis II, and blankets for permafrost. Peace talks in Miami and Kyiv's verdict on the diesel deal. Cell fates from a single snapshot, quantum links at speed, and recurrent networks that refine what they see. episodes.subject: Peace talks in Miami, a proposed fee on international students, care on the Ebola frontlines, and how sex shapes brain anatomy and behaviour
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-two hundred hours UTC on the tenth of October. Nature reports that the United States has proposed a one hundred thousand dollar charge for international students to do post-graduate work. Nature also argues that we must advocate for proper care on the frontlines of the Ebola outbreak, as the BBC reports that questions remain over an Ebola patient, a forty-year-old businessman, who flew and crossed regional borders across three nations while seriously ill. And Nature explains why Australia's bush fires got worse after British colonisation.

Ukraine and Russia. US, Ukrainian and European officials have discussed ending Russia's war at a meeting in Miami, the Kyiv Independent reports; the meeting coincided with President Trump's announcement that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States and global markets after a call with Vladimir Putin. Two EU officials had confirmed that Bjoern Seibert, Ursula von der Leyen's right-hand man, would represent the European Commission at those talks, alongside the national security advisers of France, Germany and the United Kingdom.

Frontier compute. Presolve strongly affects the performance of mixed-integer programming, and the order of its actions matters: shuffling the same sequence can inflate the slowest solve times several-fold. A new arXiv paper, ORDO, treats presolve planning as sequence generation and learns the order. Another paper finds that long-term forecasting models, used for weather and electricity planning, often give different predictions for the same moment as their input window shifts, and proposes aligning those outputs. And UniData turns simple user requirements into multimodal, multi-round instruction data for training.

Quantum desk. Nature reports the observation of relativistic bond weakening in seaborgium hexacarbonyl. On arXiv, a paper extends earlier results on how to compute when and where a quantum particle is detected, showing how absorbing boundary conditions arise as limits of complex absorbing potentials under more general assumptions. And another finds a common spectral quantisation linking a singular sextic oscillator to fractional-power potentials.

Consciousness desk. Two preprints on sex differences in the brain. One combines brain scans from nearly three thousand people across three cohorts with clinical cohorts that include sex chromosome conditions and a hormone deficiency, and reports that sex differences in subcortical anatomy are robust, already evident before puberty, and aligned with chromosomal and gonadal influences. The other finds that the sex identity of neurons in fruit flies shapes social buffering of defensive freezing behaviour.

So, this hour's receipts. A proposed fee for foreign graduates, the Ebola frontline, and fire history in Australia. Peace talks in Miami as diesel flows from Russia. Smarter solver ordering, steadier forecasts, relativistic bond weakening in seaborgium, and sex differences written into the brain. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. episodes.subject: Questions over an Ebola case, a locked-down Delhi, France's divided classrooms, Zelensky on the diesel deal, and the hidden pathology of AI upcycling
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-one hundred hours UTC on the tenth of October. Questions remain over an Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected, the BBC reports; fresh details reveal how the forty-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill. In India, thousands of security personnel have been deployed as Delhi braces for what is being called a cockroach protest; several trains to the city have been cancelled and dozens of metro stations shut to stop protesters gathering. And in France, students taking to the streets have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.

Ukraine and Russia. President Trump wrote on Truth Social that Russia will immediately supply over three hundred thousand tons of diesel to the American and global marketplace, another five hundred thousand tons in November, and one million tons after that, the Kyiv Independent reports. President Zelensky has sharply criticised President Trump's deal for Russian diesel, calling it an investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged, the BBC reports. In an analysis, the BBC's North America correspondent writes that the shock deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices, as the president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections.

Frontier compute. Mixture-of-experts models are often built by upcycling a pre-trained dense model rather than training from scratch. A new arXiv paper, DivMoE, identifies a structural pathology: when fine-grained experts all come from a single source model, routing collapses and downstream accuracy can drop to near random, so the authors compose experts across domains instead. Another paper builds a theory of how perturbations to a diffusion model's sampling path propagate into its output. And a third shows how to estimate expectations under language models more efficiently, using the next-token probabilities that sampling already produces.

Quantum desk. Nature reports the experimental observation of critical topology. On arXiv, one team studies how to simulate wavefunction flow, a formal link between generative flow models and quantum dynamics, with efficient quantum circuits. And another analyses Bhabha scattering, an electron colliding with a positron that is itself entangled with a spectator electron, to track how measurement uncertainty and entanglement are shared between the three particles.

Consciousness desk. Nature has published an editorial expression of concern about a paper titled Maternal gut bacteria promote neurodevelopmental abnormalities in mouse offspring. Nature also reports that chimpanzee and gorilla brains resist weight loss with age, unlike human brains. And it asks whether the adult brain can grow new neurons, and how researchers are solving that century-old puzzle.

So, this hour's receipts. An Ebola case that slipped across borders, a capital braced for protest, and a divided France. Zelensky's verdict on the diesel deal and the midterm politics behind it. Collapsing AI experts, perturbed diffusion models, critical topology, and an expression of concern over a gut-brain study. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. episodes.title: A Quiet Midnight: Crazy Rich Asians Returns, Adidas Sues Over Stripes & AI Scientists That Revise Their Own Equations
episodes.subject: A slow news hour: a TV revival, a four-stripes lawsuit, Ukraine's day in review, and self-correcting AI models of physics
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at midnight UTC on the tenth of October, a quiet hour on the wires. Crazy Rich Asians is returning as a television series, the BBC reports; it will pick up after the hit 2018 film and stars its original cast, Constance Wu, Henry Golding, Michelle Yeoh and Ronny Chieng. And the German sportswear brand Adidas is suing the Australian label White Fox over a four-stripes design, asking the Sydney-based company to stop selling the clothes and pay damages.

Ukraine and Russia. The Kyiv Independent's round-up of the ninth of October leads with drones striking another Yandex data center in Russia, the second damaged in two days according to the company. It also lists independent monitors' claim that twenty Russian officers were killed in Ukrainian strikes on Donetsk, the forced removal of twenty-five Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, and the closure of Russian airports. And Yuri Shvets' latest broadcast on his own channel, number twelve eighteen, is titled: the war in Ukraine is reshaping the world, Putin is losing his nuclear bluff.

Frontier compute. Building physics-based models means choosing processes, equations and couplings, decisions most AI systems cannot yet make on their own. A new arXiv paper introduces EvoSim, a self-evolving AI scientist that uses mismatches with experiments to revise its mechanisms and equations, and held-out data to test whether they are physically plausible. Another paper rethinks how language agents learn from environmental feedback when no reward is available. And the US Department of War has announced a series of initiatives to advance what it calls a New Golden Age of American science.

Quantum desk. The quantum approximate optimisation algorithm is a leading candidate for near-term hardware, but noise can bury its results. A new arXiv paper finds that how well it withstands noise depends on its variational parameters. A companion review describes adaptive workflows in which machine learning decides, instance by instance, how to formulate a problem and even whether to call a quantum processor at all. And another study finds the minimal five-party scenarios that witness a strong form of genuine multipartite nonlocality.

Consciousness desk. Population-graph models predict from brain scans by placing each person among an unlabelled cohort, so their reported accuracy can depend on how they are evaluated rather than on real predictive information. A bioRxiv study tests this on eight hundred and seventy-one subjects from twenty sites, under a protocol fixed before analysis. And a new perspective traces quantum optical sensing from diamond spin defects toward bio-integrated, fluorescent-protein spin qubits for biomedical use.

So, this hour's receipts. A film franchise reborn on television and a fight over four stripes. A day of strikes and removals in Ukraine, and a fresh broadcast on a familiar channel. AI scientists that rewrite their own physics, noise-tolerant quantum optimisation, and a warning about how brain-scan models are graded. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. episodes.title: A Tornado Tears Through Sicily, the EU's Sanctions Blind Spot & AI That Learns to Read the Room
episodes.subject: A tornado in Marsala and Petrosino, why EU sanctions miss a tank-industry company, a toss-up House race, and teaching AI the unwritten rules
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-three hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October. A huge tornado has ripped through the Sicilian town of Petrosino and the city of Marsala, the BBC reports; dramatic footage shows damage to buildings and cars. In New York, Republican congressman Mike Lawler is in a tight race for re-election in a toss-up district that could help determine control of Congress in November, NPR reports. And in India, the BBC profiles Neha Bora, one of the most recognisable faces of the country's recent Gen Z-led protests, who is taking on Modi.

Ukraine and Russia. More than four years into the full-scale war, and twelve years since Russia first invaded Ukraine, the European Union has built an extensive arsenal of sanctions, but the Kyiv Independent asks why they have missed the company behind Russia's tank industry, pointing to a persistent visibility problem that begins with two companies sharing a name. And in Kyiv, the hundred-and-fourteen-year-old Bessarabskyi Market, once a labyrinth of produce stalls, has emptied: less than a year after an upscale reopening in late 2025, most of its restaurants are gone.

Frontier compute. Voice agents are converging on a pattern in which a full-duplex model keeps talking and listening while search, reasoning and coding are delegated in the background. A new arXiv paper, DuplexAgent-RSI, builds a harness to coordinate that hand-off. Another paper, SynCo, has a self-evolving agent co-train with the system that synthesises its training tasks, so the tasks keep pace as the agent improves. And RIT-RAG lets retrieval agents navigate large document collections through trees built from the search results themselves.

Quantum desk. Experiments on photonic quantum reservoirs have reported advantages, null results and train-only effects that cannot be compared. A new arXiv paper settles the question independently of any task, finding that multi-photon interference spreads feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable particles. Another analyses the security of quantum key distribution when state preparation is imperfect. And a third develops an iterative Bayesian eigensolver that learns a ground state from single-ancilla measurements.

Consciousness desk. Human communities run on norms, from dress codes to ways of speaking, that are vast in number, change quickly and are often arbitrary. A new arXiv paper, Reading the Room, argues that aligning autonomous AI with them requires normative competence: the ability to work out, from interaction alone, which norms a community actually enforces. It sets out the foundations, design choices and open challenges for building that ability into language models.

So, this hour's receipts. A tornado in Sicily, a toss-up seat in New York, and a young protester taking on Modi. A blind spot in Europe's sanctions and an empty market hall in Kyiv. Voice agents that delegate, interference in photonic quantum reservoirs, and machines learning the unwritten rules. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Guilty Verdicts in the Murder of Two Australian Surfers, Diesel Before the Midterms & Benchmarks That Check AI's Confidence
episodes.subject: A verdict in the Robinson brothers case, how the Russian diesel deal reads in Washington and Kyiv, AI that must be calibrated, and a quick read on quantum noise
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-two hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October. Three men have been found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers, Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad, the BBC reports; their bodies were found at the bottom of a well. And Nature has two stories on the microbes we carry: how one common gut microbe protects against heart disease, and the prehistoric global migration, with humans, of gut microbes that are now vanishing.

Ukraine and Russia. NPR reports that President Trump says the United States will obtain diesel from Russia, relaxing years of US pressure on Moscow to combat prices before the midterms; he said he struck the deal with Vladimir Putin in a phone call. President Zelensky has called it a gift to Putin, saying that allowing Russia to sell petroleum products would prolong a war that must be ended. And the Kyiv Independent's daily round-up leads with drones striking another Yandex data center in Russia.

Frontier compute. Some AI systems output probabilities over fixed answers, and software acts on them through thresholds and escalation rules, so miscalibrated or wording-sensitive probabilities can trigger unintended actions with no rationale for a human to inspect. A new arXiv benchmark, TypedBench, tests these models for calibration, framing sensitivity and cost. Another paper, MedBenchAgent, goes a step further in automating medical AI evaluation: rather than only generating test items, it tries to derive the benchmark's specification itself, deciding what to evaluate and which annotations support each task.

Quantum desk. Randomised benchmarking with structured circuits scales well, but gives biased fidelity estimates at short depths, and waiting for deeper circuits can push the signal below the noise floor. A new arXiv paper overcomes this through classical post-processing alone, with a family of estimators for quickly extracting fidelity decay rates. Another team uncovers a new class of superradiant phase transition that is topologically distinct from those known before. And Nature reports on hydrogen bonding in water under extreme confinement.

Consciousness desk. Human brain assembloids let scientists study how a mutation disrupts a network. A bioRxiv study introduces a model that separates how often activity starts from how strongly past activity amplifies it, and applies it to one hundred and seventy-five recordings from assembloids carrying a MAPT mutation or its corrected version, reporting abnormal amplification over time. And another team adds six thousand three hundred and sixty-eight annotations across one thousand seven hundred and seventy-two fruit fly driver lines, to identify which neuron types each line targets.

So, this hour's receipts. Guilty verdicts in the murder of two surfers and their friend, and the microbes that travel with us. Diesel from Russia ahead of the midterms, and Kyiv's objection. Calibration tests for AI that acts on probabilities, faster quantum benchmarks, and abnormal amplification in mutant brain networks. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. So, this hour's receipts. A Nobel for Navi Pillay, a farewell to Nana Patekar, and an Afghan couple remembering. A recalled envoy, a prisoner-of-war row, and a loss count from Kyiv. paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-one hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The War Department announced a series of initiatives to advance the President's vision of a new golden age of American science. NPR talks to White House correspondent April Ryan about decades of pressing presidents for answers, and how asking questions put her in the President's crosshairs. And NPR reports on how documentary director Alex Gibney became a critic of Elon Musk, drawing on a trove of documents and interviews with people close to him.

Ukraine and beyond. The acclaimed Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach has been detained by Austrian authorities in Vienna, the Kyiv Independent reports; he was reportedly there on an editorial assignment with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko. Actor Serhii Strelnikov, who played a special forces commander in this year's thriller Killhouse, has enlisted in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces. And in Chile, residents were airlifted to safety after the Mapocho river burst its banks following unusually heavy rain, the BBC reports.

Frontier compute. When should you correct an AI agent, at which step, and how? A new arXiv paper steered agents at every step with four different mechanisms and ran each version to the end, about eighty-two thousand counterfactual outcomes, to test whether the agent's own uncertainty is a good guide. Another paper asks which save points are worth keeping when coding agents work, measuring how much a checkpoint actually cuts the cost of recovering from a mistake.

Quantum, and life. Superconducting qubits use only the two lowest energy levels of a circuit, and information easily leaks into higher ones. A new arXiv paper uses geodesic-based optimal control to suppress that leakage. Another team tests quantum kernel methods for spotting anomalies in real malware beaconing data, weighing performance against how far each kernel departs from classical ones. And Nature reveals how a common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

Consciousness desk. Can you think pain down? A new bioRxiv study reanalysed more than three thousand heat-stimulation trials from thirty-three participants told to turn their pain up or down. Both instructions shifted ratings the intended way, and turning pain down came with lower activity in the brain's secondary sensory areas. And Nature asks a century-old question: can your brain grow new neurons, and how are researchers solving the puzzle?

So, this hour's receipts. A golden-age promise for American science, and a reporter recalling life in the President's crosshairs. A Ukrainian journalist detained in Vienna, an actor turned drone soldier, and a river over its banks in Chile. Agents that need to know when to be corrected, qubits that leak, and a mind that can turn its own pain down. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. In Madrid, hundreds have pitched tents in the city centre, blaming vulture funds for Spain's housing crisis, the BBC reports, as the prime minister calls a snap election. In Rome, Italy approved an overhaul of its elections; Prime Minister Meloni says it will bring stable government, and the opposition calls it a scam to keep her in power. And Israel says most British diplomats will leave the East Jerusalem consulate, after it promised to respond to UK sanctions on settlements.

Ukraine and Russia. Addressing Ukrainian attacks on a Russian data centre, President Zelensky said, we always respond in kind, adding that Russia has been and still is striking Ukraine's data centres. Nature asks what scientists know about the plague scare in Russia, and what Moscow won't say. And Yuri Shvets has posted broadcast number twelve eighteen, titled: the war in Ukraine is reshaping the world, Putin is losing his nuclear bluff.

Frontier compute. Security teams turn threat reports into precise detection rules, and general-purpose language models often get those rules wrong, with invalid syntax, wrong log sources and logic that is far too broad. A new arXiv paper presents Sigma-Hunter, a model tuned for exactly that job. Another paper returns to John Rawls and his original position, the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice without knowing your own place in society, and asks whether large language models can offer a view from everywhere.

Quantum, and life. A new arXiv paper produces photon pairs in a lithium niobate waveguide resonator with close to two gigahertz of bandwidth in the telecom band, and measures their correlations mode by mode. Another team cross-checks two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, and finds that different assumptions can give different answers to the same basic tasks. And from Nature: big dogs age faster than little ones, and rogue jumping genes might be to blame.

Consciousness desk. How does a network of neurons organise itself? A new bioRxiv preprint introduces connectomics by sequencing, combining barcoded rabies tracing with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct more than ten thousand neural networks inside cerebral organoids. Another study, across one hundred and seventy-five recordings of brain assembloids carrying MAPT mutations, finds abnormal amplification of activity over time, separating how often activity starts from how strongly it feeds on itself.

So, this hour's receipts. Tents in Madrid and a snap election. A vote overhaul in Rome. Ukraine answering data centre with data centre, and a plague scare Russia will not explain. A security model that writes cleaner rules, a philosopher's thought experiment handed to machines, and more than ten thousand organoid networks mapped by sequencing. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at nineteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The Kyiv Independent reports President Zelensky is sending a delegation to meet the Trump administration's envoys over two days, and is counting on a European team to join, as he hints at secret US-Russia economic talks. The same paper carries an open letter on the administration's invitation to Vladimir Putin for December's G20 summit in Miami, arguing it should come with conditions. And NPR finds both parties spending heavily in some sixty House districts that could decide control of the chamber.

Russia and its neighbours. Russia has lifted the quarantine in the Irkutsk region, the Kyiv Independent reports, where a twenty-eight-year-old worker at the Anti-Plague Institute, Darya Shipilova, allegedly died of plague; initial reports raised fears of pneumonic plague after a laboratory accident. And in Chisinau, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said that if this winter in Ukraine is as hard as the world expects, Moldova is ready to receive as many people as need safety.

Frontier compute. When AI agents share a reward for finished tasks, reporting unsafe work costs the reporter. A new arXiv paper studies a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting, and asks whether training can teach a silent team to speak up. Another paper looks at looped language models, which promise to save memory and compute on easy words, and finds the current open models fail to deliver it in practice.

Quantum, and life. Error correction is the price of a useful quantum computer. A new arXiv paper builds codes with three logical qubits whose CCZ gate is applied transversally, using projective geometry for the structure and a SAT solver to find the rest, at thirteen sizes from forty-eight to four hundred and ninety-six qubits. Another paper defines quantum versions of the classes that grade how well hard optimisation problems can be approximated. And Nature captures how to build a mouse, embryo development in stunning detail.

Consciousness desk. Cortical organoids, small lab-grown pieces of brain tissue, reproduce key steps of development. A new bioRxiv preprint presents a flexible three-dimensional interface that reveals functional subnetworks and coordinated circuit activity inside them. Another asks how the brain gives credit: when an action pays off, how does the signal find its way back from the basal ganglia and cerebellum, through the thalamus, to the cortical circuits that chose it?

So, this hour's receipts. A Ukrainian delegation heading to Trump's envoys, and an invitation for Putin to Miami. A quarantine lifted in Irkutsk after a lab worker's suspected plague death. Moldova bracing for a hard winter next door. Agents learning to blow the whistle, and organoids lighting up in three dimensions. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: a proposed $100,000 charge for international students to work after graduating in the US, deportations to African countries, an ICE warehouse in New Jersey, Kyiv plunged into near-total darkness, Operation Vivaldi near Lyman, a tanker hit off Qatar, AI agents whose rejected ideas come back as facts, small models versus frontier models, a picture of two qubits, NASA's Artemis II Moon data, and how one brain region juggles many tasks.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at eighteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. Nature reports the United States has proposed a one hundred thousand dollar charge for international students who want to do post-graduate work there. Human Rights Watch says more than five hundred migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, and calls the deportations unlawful. And NPR investigated rumours in northern New Jersey that ICE has quietly used a warehouse as a detention centre all summer; neighbours say it has.

Ukraine. Russian attacks plunged Kyiv into near-total darkness, the Kyiv Independent reports. The drop in voltage halted metro trains and escalators and disrupted power and water across the capital. On the front, the paper goes inside Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast fought with drones above and robots below; Russian officials claim to control Lyman, and Ukrainian infantry tell a different story. In the Gulf, the BBC reports an oil and chemical tanker hit by multiple projectiles off Qatar, with casualties reported on board.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper names a quiet failure in AI agents with long-term memory. While thinking, an agent may consider a plan, imagine a tool result or repeat someone else's belief, then reject it. If memory keeps only the sentences, those discarded possibilities can come back later as facts. A second paper tested nine models, from tiny to frontier, inside a working home-automation system, and asks why one big model should serve every call when the jobs differ tenfold in difficulty.

Quantum and space. Entanglement is notoriously hard to picture. A new arXiv paper proposes a simple image for any pure two-qubit state: two Bloch balls, one for each qubit, plus a reflection-rotation and a contraction that carry the entanglement, and proves the picture has no gaps. Another team studies entangling gates between two species of atoms in neutral-atom quantum computers. And Nature reports NASA has released a trove of Moon data from the historic Artemis two flight.

Consciousness desk. How does one patch of brain do several jobs at once? A new bioRxiv preprint offers a theory of multi-tasking, starting from the idea that activity during each task lies on its own low-dimensional manifold, and sorts competing models by their assumptions. Another study recorded EEG while adults passively heard and saw small numbers, testing whether the brain detects changes in quantity before attention arrives, by ear and by eye.

So, this hour's receipts. A six-figure price on staying to work after graduation. Five hundred deportations to Africa, and a warehouse that neighbours say became a detention centre. A capital without light, metro or water, and robots on the Lyman front. Agents whose rejected thoughts return as facts, a picture of entanglement, and a brain that runs many tasks at once. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: new torture-conspiracy charges against Nicolás Maduro, a $1.5 billion US health deal with Zambia, a shrinking regulator for crypto and prediction markets, the drone barrage on Kyiv, South Korea recalling its Ukraine envoy, Ukraine's strike on the Salavat refinery, a failure-mode map of catastrophic AI risk, measuring how AI agents learn, quantum forecasts no classical learner can match, heat pumped on a quantum chip, the UAE's asteroid probe, and how long a perceptual moment lasts from infancy to adulthood.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at seventeen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The BBC reports that Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro has been charged with conspiracy to commit torture, over the alleged torture of US citizens held in Venezuela while he was in power. Zambia has signed a one and a half billion dollar health deal with the United States, negotiated after the President cut USAID funding. And NPR reports that as crypto and prediction markets expand, the agency meant to write their rules has seen its staff and enforcement actions drop sharply.

Ukraine. A Russian drone barrage on Kyiv killed four people and injured nineteen, the Kyiv Independent reports, and disrupted electricity and water; the energy firm DTEK announced emergency shutdowns around the capital. Across the country, Ukraine's Air Force counted one hundred and forty-two Shahed-type drones overnight, eighty-two of them jet-powered. South Korea is recalling its envoy to Ukraine after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners of war were transferred to Seoul. And Ukraine's General Staff confirms a hit on the Salavat refinery, one of Russia's largest, some thirteen hundred kilometres from the front.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper maps how advanced AI could lead to human extinction or permanent disempowerment, and argues it would take no consciousness and no hostility, only interacting failures: misalignment, harmful use, organisational failure and competitive deployment. A second paper asks a simpler question with large consequences: not what an agent can do today, but how well it learns from its own mistakes.

Quantum and space. Can an agent's forecasts reveal whether it reasons with a quantum model? A new arXiv paper says yes: quantum Bayesian retrodiction can make predictions no classical learner could match, but only for measurements with more than four outcomes. On real hardware, another team ran geometric heat pumping on a superconducting quantum processor, moving energy between reservoirs at the same temperature. And Nature reports the UAE has completed the Arab world's first solo space probe, now on course for an asteroid.

Consciousness desk. Perception feels continuous, but evidence suggests the brain stitches sensory input into short windows of time. A new bioRxiv study measured how long those windows last, from five months of age to adulthood, across three hundred and eight participants, using eye tracking that needs no instructions. How the length of a perceptual moment develops through childhood had, until now, been unknown.

So, this hour's receipts. Torture charges for a deposed president. Kyiv losing power and water under drones. A diplomatic rift over prisoners of war, and a refinery burning far behind the front. A map of how AI could fail us without ever meaning to. Quantum forecasts no classical learner can make, and the length of a single moment of human awareness. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at sixteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. Washington first, and it is a quantum day. The War Department announced new initiatives and programme updates worth about three hundred and fifty million dollars to strengthen US quantum computing for national security. Its Office of Strategic Capital also signed a one hundred and fifty million dollar conditional loan commitment with PsiQuantum, for manufacturing and prototyping in the United States. And NPR reports the President wants to turn one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat, sort of a Camp David, he said.

Ukraine. The Kyiv Independent reports at least thirty-three dead after a Russian glide bomb struck buses in Kramatorsk. On diplomacy, both Washington and Moscow now confirm the latest peace push is falling apart; Secretary of State Rubio said there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement. Ukraine's General Staff confirms a strike on Russia's Omsk oil refinery, deep in Siberia. An investigation into the mass Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace on September ninth found Polish SIM cards inside the downed Russian drones. And Britain ramped up sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet, its crypto industry and big oil.

Frontier compute, and a farewell. Margaret Hamilton has died at ninety, the BBC reports. She led the software for NASA's Apollo missions, the code that helped land Apollo eleven on the Moon. Today's arXiv asks whether AI agents can do open-ended science, testing them in Station, a world where many agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. Another paper probes how fragile safety is in language models running on our own devices, and whether it hangs on a small set of parameters.

Quantum. A new arXiv paper tries to unite two ideas about how the past gets written into the world. Decoherent histories asks which past events leave formal records. Quantum Darwinism asks which present facts get copied redundantly into the environment. Neither implies the other. The authors build a bridge on one insight: only redundant records of past events count. A second paper shows how a programmable two-qubit gate can be teleported, with a third party holding the program.

Consciousness desk. A new bioRxiv preprint maps how five psychedelics, LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and five-MeO-DMT, restructure the way information is stored, transferred and transformed across the human cortex, in eighty participants. And in monkeys, wireless recordings from the high-level visual cortex ask whether the brain replays what it saw while awake during REM-like sleep. The preprint's title answers: neural signatures of food come back while they sleep.

So, this hour's receipts. Half a billion dollars of Pentagon quantum money and loans. Thirty-three dead on buses in Kramatorsk, and a peace push that both sides now call finished. Refineries burning in Siberia, Polish SIM cards in Russian drones. A goodbye to the woman whose code reached the Moon. And brains that keep rewriting themselves, awake, asleep or on psychedelics. paragraphs: Welcome back to ZeroFilter. It is midnight UTC on the eighth of October. Washington first. The BBC reports that President Trump will speak to Vladimir Putin about the death of a plague lab worker in Russia. Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague have prompted calls for more transparency from Moscow. Also tonight, the War Department's Office of Strategic Capital announced a one and a half billion dollar conditional loan commitment to Wolfspeed, an American manufacturer of semiconductor materials. Conditional is the word to watch.

To Ukraine and its neighbours. The Kyiv Independent reports that a Russian attack on Pryluky killed at least twenty people, five of them children, on a day of strikes that fell on Putin's seventy-fourth birthday. Danish intelligence says Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, increasingly aiming at targets tied to Western military support for Ukraine. Lithuania will deploy troops along its border with Kaliningrad, a preventative step, its interior minister said, against signals that Russia may announce mobilization. And EU ambassadors waved through the largest-ever list of Russia sanctions, reaching shipyards, aviation, electronics and aerospace firms. Yuri Shvets titled his latest broadcast, number twelve seventeen: Ukraine is striking Russia systematically, Europe is lifting its nuclear taboos.

Frontier compute. Nature reports that OpenAI has posted seven hundred mathematics preprints online, and that mathematicians are up in arms. The same issue carries a paper on retrofitting language models to operate over bytes, which Nature's news desk summed up in one headline: the retrofitted model can count the letter i in artificial intelligence. Models that read text in chunks called tokens have long stumbled on spelling questions exactly like that one.

Precision physics. Nuclear clocks are ticking for the first time, Nature reports. Two papers describe a thorium two twenty-nine optical nuclear clock with a feedback loop, and a nuclear clock synchronized to thorium two twenty-nine. Atomic clocks count the rhythm of electrons. A nuclear clock listens to a transition inside the nucleus itself, far better shielded from the noise of the outside world, which is why physicists have chased one for decades.

Consciousness desk. A new bioRxiv study followed people as they drifted from wakefulness toward sleep while locating sounds and touches, with EEG tracking their alertness moment to moment. Drowsiness slowed their responses and made them miss more trials. But when they answered, they stayed largely accurate, and agreeing or conflicting touch signals kept shaping their choices. The authors report that this decision-making persists as alertness fades, even when no overt response comes. The mind keeps working the problem while awareness dims.

So, tonight's receipts. A suspected plague death that made it onto a presidential call list. A conditional loan for American chip materials. Twenty dead in Pryluky, sabotage in Denmark, troops on the Kaliningrad line and Europe's biggest sanctions list yet. Seven hundred maths preprints from OpenAI, a model that can finally count its letters, and clocks that tick inside the nucleus. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Pentagon Advisers' Conflicts, a Tanker Ablaze off Sochi & a Blueprint for Quantum Gravity
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: ethics worries over Elon Musk's and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles, the War Department's counter-drone laser and microwave picks, a shadow-fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Sochi, Ukraine's drone-casualty tally, Yuri Shvets' broadcast #1216, error-correcting dynamics inside language models, a proposed test of gravity-induced entanglement, and how the brain recalibrates what feels simultaneous.
paragraphs: Welcome back to ZeroFilter. It is twenty-two hundred hours UTC. In Washington, NPR reports that Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey have taken new Pentagon roles, and ethics experts are worried: their companies, SpaceX and Anduril, could benefit from recommendations in a Pentagon study on future autonomous weapons. Same day, the War Department named the laser and microwave systems it selected after its JIATF 401 counter-drone pilot. My take: when the people advising on the shopping list also sell the merchandise, that is a conflict of interest.

To the Black Sea. The Kyiv Independent reports a shadow-fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Sochi, and Russian Telegram channels suggest sea drones hit it. Robert Brovdi, call sign Madyar, who commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, says his units recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded from October 1 to 5, up from 1,931 in the same days of September. And in broadcast number 1216, Yuri Shvets lays out what he calls six priorities for victory: six lines of effort that must work at once, instead of slogans and promises of another counteroffensive.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper asks why language models stay coherent even when you shove their internal activations around, for example with steering. The authors' hypothesis is passive error correction: mechanisms in the forward pass that funnel activations back toward regions that produce sensible output, which the title calls privileged error-correcting basins. If that holds up, these models are sturdier than the parrot jokes suggest. That last part is my read, not their claim.

Quantum next. Nobody has yet caught gravity entangling two masses. Proposals argue that if gravity alone can do it, gravity itself must be quantum, and with the Planck scale out of reach, a tabletop interferometer is the realistic back door. A new arXiv paper works out the best interferometer geometry for that experiment. No result yet. This is a blueprint, not a discovery.

Consciousness desk. Your sense of at the same time is not fixed. A new bioRxiv study looks at rapid temporal recalibration: after signals from different senses arrive slightly out of sync, your judgment of what is simultaneous shifts toward that recent timing. The authors separate a genuine perceptual realignment from a decision-level carryover from your previous answers, and report that the two come apart across the senses. Part of what feels like perception is bookkeeping.
